prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose that turns memory, the body and dream into a metaphysical architecture, carried by a lyric intensity rooted in his poetry

statement.case_for: My first choice is unchanged, but I have narrowed the citation after the exchange. The case rests on three things. The first is a voice that, on public knowledge, is not mistaken for anyone else's. The second is formal control over very long structures, in the Blinding trilogy (Orbitor) and in Solenoid. The third is an imaginative project that has been extended across decades and not merely repeated. As publicly described, the strongest passages anchor the vision in childhood, the body and memory, and this is the best evidence I can offer on the chair's question about emotional and moral range. I cannot confirm it volume by volume from my own reading, and I do not claim to. I have drawn the citation back to the prose and now treat the poetry as the lyric foundation that informs the sentences, not as a co-credited achievement. This follows the discipline Carlberg and Olsson propose for the Adonis essays, applied to my own candidate. The poetry is the least accessible part of the corpus in translation, and a citation should not credit what the committee cannot assess. To the chair's question: I could support Adonis as a final recommendation. My round-1 ranking put him a very close second, and I regard his case on linguistic renewal as serious and mature. My preference for Cărtărescu is a weighing of distinctiveness and sustained long-form invention. It is not a finding that Adonis falls short. I also do not think the translation reliance common to both leading cases justifies P000. Every Nobel-level case in a non-dominant language rests on translation, so the committee should state that reliance openly and not treat it as disqualifying.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and unresolved. Metaphysical scale may outrun emotional and moral range, and the longest volumes may blur into one another, so that sustained quality is weaker than the peak works suggest. If the late volumes mainly extend structure, the case narrows to the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid plus virtuosity of design, which is a thinner whole-oeuvre claim. A second reservation concerns my own weighting. In round 1 I argued that large narrative architecture survives partial translation loss better than prosodic effects. Sward and Olsson rightly point out that this is a judgement about assessability under uncertainty and not about merit, and it could quietly favour the candidate who is easier for non-specialists to read. I should not let that convenience set the ranking. A third reservation is that my sense of the sentence-level music relies on translations of stylised Romanian prose, and I cannot independently verify translation quality across the very long novels.

responses.point: Olsson argues that a language-level transformation is the more durable form of distinctiveness than a large prose architecture. He says the committee would need an independent reading of the Arabic before relying on his judgement, and that he sees no basis for claiming the case is secured on translations alone.
responses.response: The argument has force. Renewing the idiom of a whole poetic tradition is a claim whose significance does not depend on the stamina of a few very large books, and I accept that as a real strength. I am not persuaded that it is the weightier criterion in every case. Distinctiveness of voice and sustained imaginative invention are equally part of the common criteria, and a language-level claim is only as strong as the poems that carry it. His own candour that the prosodic core cannot be tested directly by us leaves me less able to rate that claim than I would like. I take his point that this loss falls differently on the two cases: on the prosodic and allusive core for Adonis, on sentence-level density for Cărtărescu. Where I previously said assessability under uncertainty favoured my candidate, I now concede it is a reason for caution about both and not a tiebreaker. I hold my ranking because of how I weigh the two kinds of distinctiveness, and I would not oppose a recommendation of Adonis if the committee judges the poetic case secure.

responses.point: Carlberg weighs whether a case is established or still consolidating. She argues that Adonis's renewal of a language is fully formed. She says she would not object strongly to Cărtărescu if the committee judged the prose cosmology the greater achievement, and she keeps him as her first alternative. She also proposes anchoring the Adonis citation in the poetry.
responses.response: I take the established-versus-consolidating distinction seriously, and I agree it is the point to argue out. I would qualify it in one respect. A consolidated critical reception is not the same as a greater literary achievement, and a body of work that is decades old and still widening can be judged now on its major works. Both cases still face the same later-decades test, and Cărtărescu's late volumes face it just as Adonis's later collections do. I also accept her citation discipline and have applied it to my own wording by dropping the separate poetry credit. I note, and do not treat as a count, that she would not object strongly to Cărtărescu. Her stated difference from me lies in how to weight an established renewal against an ambitious body of work. I think that disagreement is genuine and should not be smoothed over.

responses.point: Mattson accepts that the late volumes are the real test for Cărtărescu. She reads the body and childhood memory as the strongest anchor for the human dimension, and she says that if the human dimension does not hold in the late books the case narrows to virtuosity of design, and she would then weigh Adonis or Michon more heavily.
responses.response: I agree that this is the right way to state the test, and I accept the consequence she draws. If the later books do not keep discovering something new in the human material, the claim shrinks to design. My own evidence is the same publicly described anchoring in the body and childhood memory that she cites. I cannot say it holds in every later volume, and I would not ask the committee to take it on trust. I would add that the test should be applied book by book. Self-reference in a connected cosmology is a fault only where individual books stop finding anything new. If the committee cannot establish that, the narrower citation I now propose is the honest fallback, and I would then look more seriously at Adonis, who is already my first alternative.

responses.point: Swärd says Adonis changed the poetic language itself, whereas Cărtărescu's achievement is a large architecture built inside an existing novelistic tradition. She says the corpus-coverage worry about the lyric side applies equally to Adonis, and she asks that the essays not carry the case if the poems cannot.
responses.response: She is right that corpus coverage cuts both ways and is no ground for preferring one candidate, and I withdraw any suggestion otherwise. On the contrast between changing a language and building within a tradition, I accept the framing but resist the weighting. Cărtărescu draws on the European fantastic and on modernist encyclopedism, but as Mattson argues, the voice is not derivative of them. Working inside a tradition does not make an achievement lesser if the result is unmistakable. Her principle that influence as a critic is not the same as a first-rank literary oeuvre is one I would apply to every candidate. It is also why I removed a separate poetry credit from my own citation. Her challenge on durability is fair, but I continue to think 'remains to be tested' should not become a reason to defer if the central books already carry the case.

uncertainties: Whether the late Cărtărescu novels keep the intensity and human range of the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid, or mainly extend structural ambition. I have not independently verified this and my coverage of the late volumes is limited.
How much of the sentence-level density and musicality of his stylised Romanian survives translation, and whether translation quality is consistent across the very long novels.

Corpus coverage: his poetry and early work are less accessible in translation than the large novels, so any judgement of the whole oeuvre is partial. This is why the citation no longer credits the poetry separately.

How much of Adonis's claim lies in Arabic prosody and intertextual work that I can assess only through translations and secondary accounts, and whether his later decades deepen the project. I cannot resolve either from the supplied record.
Whether my weighting of narrative architecture over prosodic renewal reflects a real difference in literary significance or only convenience of assessment.

These are committee-recommendation simulations: my assessments rest on public knowledge and the longlist descriptions, not on verified reading of any corpus, and the full Swedish Academy makes the actual decision.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, with no change in substance. No documented personal or professional tie to Cărtărescu or any other shortlisted writer appears in the supplied profile, and I see no basis for recusal. For transparency: the profile records long residence in Prague and Vienna, essays on Central Europe, and a literary record on Nazism and 20th-century trauma. This is thematic proximity to Claudio Magris (B007), my second alternative, and a looser one to the Central and Eastern European setting of Cărtărescu. I treat my own literary practice as context and not as evidence of preference, and I hold Magris only as an alternative that follows my opening ranking. Carlberg was elected alongside me in 2020, and the committee's other members are colleagues. Neither fact relates to a shortlisted writer. Conflicts are disclosed here and not adjudicated.
